Subject to any international management / trade controls

documentation.range: This Australian endemic species is widely distributed along coasts, ranges, slopes, and adjacent plains of eastern and southeastern Australia, from southeastern South Australia to Cape York Peninsula, Queensland (Cogger 2014).
documentation.population: It is a very common species, with a seemingly stable population.
documentation.habitats: This species occurs in well-timbered areas from dry woodlands to cool temperate southern forests (Wilson and Swan 2013). It is a large arboreal lizard that is a major predator of nestling birds; individuals also feed on carrion, insects, reptiles and small mammals (Cogger 2014). While they may forage in disturbed areas, including suburban yards, this is a woodland species and are only found in disturbed areas adjacent to suitable bushland habitat (M. Greenlees pers. comm. 2017). Females lay a clutch of 6-12 eggs, usually within termite nests; young hatch and emerge from the nest 6-8 weeks later (Cogger 2014).
documentation.threats: There are no substantial threats to this species. Complete clearance of trees and vegetation would be the only threat to this fairly adaptable species.
documentation.measures: This species is listed as Vulnerable in Victoria under the Wildlife Act 1975, and is considered to be Rare in South Australia under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1972 (Department of Primary Industries, Parks, Water and Environment 2014) and it is listed in CITES Appendix II. It is present in many protected areas. No direct conservation measures are needed.
documentation.use_trade: This species is of some limited interest to the pet trade.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern, because the species has a wide distribution with no threats, it is adaptable and there are no ongoing population declines.
